meta.titre: Measurement: SI units, instruments and scalars and vectors

sections.contenu_markdown: A tailor in Bafoussam measures a customer with a tape, a trader sells palm oil by the litre and a market scale gives the mass of a bag of maize. Every one of these jobs needs the right instrument, a good reading and the right unit. The GCE regularly asks for SI units, for conversions such as degrees Celsius to kelvin, for scalar and vector quantities, and for readings from simple instruments. A careless unit or a wrong reading can cost marks in every paper.

items: The metre rule, the stopwatch and the measuring cylinder are used to measure length, time and volume.
Decimal prefixes such as kilo, centi and milli change the size of a unit by powers of 10.
A scale is read with the eye directly above the mark to avoid error.

sections.titre: SI units, instruments, readings and quantities
sections.contenu_markdown:
**SI base units.** length: metre (m); mass: kilogram (kg); time: second (s); electric current: ampere (A); temperature: kelvin (K). Other units are derived from them, for example area $\mathrm{m^2}$, volume $\mathrm{m^3}$, speed $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, density $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and force $\mathrm{N} = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

**Prefixes.** kilo (k) $= 10^{3}$; centi (c) $= 10^{-2}$; milli (m) $= 10^{-3}$; micro ($\mu$) $= 10^{-6}$. For example $1\ \mathrm{km} = 1\,000\ \mathrm{m}$ and $1\ \mathrm{m^3} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

**Instruments.**

| Instrument | Measures | Smallest division (reading to) |
|---|---|---|
| Metre rule | length | $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ |
| Vernier callipers | length, diameter | $0.1\ \mathrm{mm}$ |
| Micrometer screw gauge | thickness of a wire | $0.01\ \mathrm{mm}$ |
| Measuring cylinder | volume of a liquid | usually $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ |
| Stopwatch | time | $0.1\ \mathrm{s}$ or $0.01\ \mathrm{s}$ |

To read a scale correctly, put your eye level with the mark (avoid *parallax error*) and check for zero error. Read water at the bottom of its meniscus. Repeat a reading and take the average to reduce random error.

**Scalars and vectors.** A scalar has size only: mass, distance, speed, time, energy, temperature. A vector has size and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight.

**Temperature scales.** $T/\mathrm{K} = \theta/^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273$. The lower fixed point of a thermometer (melting ice) is $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C} = 273\ \mathrm{K}$. The upper fixed point (steam above boiling water at standard pressure) is $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C} = 373\ \mathrm{K}$.

variantes.nom: Reading vernier callipers and a micrometer
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes a scale reading in words or gives a table of divisions.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Vernier callipers (0.1 mm):** main scale reading just before the zero of the vernier + vernier division in line with a main scale mark $\times$ 0.01 cm. Example: $2.4\ \mathrm{cm}$ on the main scale and the 6th vernier division in line gives $2.4 + 0.06 = 2.46\ \mathrm{cm}$. **Micrometer (0.01 mm):** sleeve reading + thimble reading $\times$ 0.01 mm. Example: sleeve $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ and thimble $28$ divisions gives $5.5 + 0.28 = 5.78\ \mathrm{mm}$.

variantes.nom: Distance and displacement; speed and velocity
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a body does not move in a straight line.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Distance is the length of the path travelled (a scalar). Displacement is the straight-line distance from the start to the end, with its direction (a vector). Average speed $=$ distance $\div$ time; average velocity $=$ displacement $\div$ time.

variantes.nom: Measuring a small quantity by repeating
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the quantity is too small or too quick to measure once.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Measure many repeats and divide: the period of a pendulum is found from the time for 20 oscillations divided by 20, which reduces the effect of reaction time. The thickness of one sheet of paper is found from the thickness of a pile divided by the number of sheets.

sections.enonce_markdown: A student wants the density of an irregular stone. A balance reading to $0.1\ \mathrm{g}$ gives its mass as $31.2\ \mathrm{g}$. The stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder: the water level rises from $40\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ to $52\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. Find the volume of the stone and its density in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

etapes.justification: The stone pushes aside a volume of water equal to its own volume.
Density is mass per unit volume.
Both quantities are in the units given by the instruments, so the first result is in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.
$1\ \mathrm{g} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $1\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^3}$, so the number is multiplied by $1\,000$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The stone has a volume of $12\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ and a density of $2.6\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, that is $2\,600\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.

items.pourquoi_faux: To change from Celsius to kelvin, 273 is added, not subtracted. A kelvin value cannot be negative.

items.erreur_markdown: "I read the measuring cylinder from above the top of the meniscus."
items.pourquoi_faux: A reading from the wrong position gives a parallax error. For water the reading is at the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye at the same level.
items.correction_markdown: Put your eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.

items.pourquoi_faux: A cubic metre is $100 \times 100 \times 100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. Prefix factors for area and volume must be raised to powers.

items.erreur_markdown: "The SI base unit of mass is the gram."
items.pourquoi_faux: The SI base unit is the kilogram. The gram is a smaller unit.
items.correction_markdown: Use the kilogram (kg) in formulas such as $W = mg$ and $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

items.erreur_markdown: "A man walks 6 km north and 8 km east, so his displacement is 14 km."
items.pourquoi_faux: $14\ \mathrm{km}$ is the distance. Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to end, found by Pythagoras, and has a direction.

items.enonce_markdown: Convert: (a) $4.5\ \mathrm{km}$ to metres; (b) $750\ \mathrm{g}$ to kilograms; (c) $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to kelvin; (d) $320\ \mathrm{K}$ to degrees Celsius.

(a) A micrometer screw gauge has $5.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ showing on the sleeve and the thimble is at the 28th division. Each thimble division is $0.01\ \mathrm{mm}$. Find the reading. (b) A pupil times 20 swings of a pendulum three times and gets $28.4\ \mathrm{s}$, $28.6\ \mathrm{s}$ and $28.2\ \mathrm{s}$. Find the period of the pendulum. (c) Why is it better to time 20 swings rather than one?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Reading $= 5.5 + 28 \times 0.01 = 5.5 + 0.28 = \mathbf{5.78\ mm}$.

(b) Mean time for 20 swings $= \dfrac{28.4 + 28.6 + 28.2}{3} = \dfrac{85.2}{3} = 28.4\ \mathrm{s}$. Period $= \dfrac{28.4}{20} = \mathbf{1.42\ s}$.

(c) The error from starting and stopping the stopwatch (reaction time) is about the same for 1 swing or 20 swings, so it becomes a much smaller fraction of the total time.

items.enonce_markdown: A man walks $6\ \mathrm{km}$ due north and then $8\ \mathrm{km}$ due east in a total time of $2\ \mathrm{h}$. Find (a) the distance travelled, (b) his displacement, (c) his average speed, (d) his average velocity, and (e) say which of these are vectors.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Distance $= 6 + 8 = \mathbf{14\ km}$.

(b) The two legs are at right angles, so displacement $= \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = \mathbf{10\ km}$, in a direction $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{8}{6} \approx 53^\circ$ east of north.

(c) Average speed $= \dfrac{14}{2} = \mathbf{7\ km\,h^{-1}}$.

(d) Average velocity $= \dfrac{10}{2} = \mathbf{5\ km\,h^{-1}}$ at $53^\circ$ east of north.

(e) **Displacement and velocity** are vectors. Distance and speed are scalars.

items_markdown: SI base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere and kelvin; use kilograms and metres in formulas.
Prefixes: kilo $10^{3}$, centi $10^{-2}$, milli $10^{-3}$, micro $10^{-6}$; volume conversions need the cube of the length factor.
Read scales with your eye level with the mark, check zero error and repeat to average; use the bottom of the meniscus for water.
Scalars have only size (mass, distance, speed, energy); vectors have size and direction (displacement, velocity, force, weight).
$T/\mathrm{K} = \theta/^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273$: the lower fixed point is $273\ \mathrm{K}$ and the upper fixed point is $373\ \mathrm{K}$.
